claims.text: A controlled thermomechanical protocol can simultaneously improve yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance in high-entropy alloys relative to conventional processing.
AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is an example alloy that can be produced by conventional casting and thermomechanical processing.
Controlled rolling followed by rapid annealing will trigger a deformation-induced phase transformation.
The deformation-induced phase transformation will create a dual-phase lamellar architecture.
Rolling and rapid annealing will enhance local chemical order.
An ultrafine duplex lamellar microstructure can be formed in AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
The desired architecture contains a ductile, lower-modulus phase dispersed within a stiff, high-modulus matrix.
Engineered local chemical order will be concentrated at the phase boundaries of the lamellar structure.
Fine lamellae and their phase boundaries strengthen the alloy.
Ductility is preserved because the ductile phase promotes enhanced dislocation mobility.
A stiff second phase increases the overall Young’s modulus of the dual-phase alloy.
Lamellar interfaces arrest cracks and thereby improve fracture resistance.
Dynamic local chemical order can contribute to high yield strength and work hardening through dislocation cross-slip, transformation, and twinning.
The proposed microstructure will simultaneously improve yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
Each of the four mechanical properties is expected to improve by approximately 10–20% relative to state-of-the-art conventional HEAs.
Conventional microstructural refinement often improves strength at the expense of ductility.
The benefits require maintenance of the desired phase stability across room-temperature, moderately elevated-temperature, quasi-static, and dynamic loading conditions.
Insufficient transformation, failure to establish local chemical order, or destabilization of the dual-phase structure will negate the predicted improvements.
